extracted.intended_audience: general readers / students of Rabelais and early-modern satirical literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted prescriptive counsel and practical criteria embedded in Rabelais' narrative about whether Panurge should marry — covering decision‑making, spouse selection, and five medical/social remedies for controlling sexual desire. The page is a satirical early‑modern treatment but contains explicit 'rules' and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-determination in the marriage decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone in the project and enterprise of marriage ought to be his own carver, sole arbitrator of his proper thoughts, and from himself alone take counsel in the main and peremptory closure of what his determination should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel (via Raminagrobis) argues that the individual should make the ultimate choice about marriage rather than relying entirely on others; beware philauty (self‑love) which can blind judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult relevant experts for distinct human goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever we are, or have, consisteth in three things—the soul, the body, and the goods. For the preservation of these three, there are three sorts of learned men ordained: theologues for the soul, physicians for the welfare of the body, and lawyers for the safety of our goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: assemble a theologian, physician, and lawyer to confer on a difficult personal question (Pantagruel proposes also a philosopher as an able assistant able to resolve doubts). The passage prescribes which specialist to consult for what domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: First introspect: consult yourself and assess bodily state
rubrics_metrics.description: Before taking counsel, 'first you must consult with yourself. Do you find any trouble or disquiet in your body by the importunate stings and pricklings of the flesh?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee counsels self-examination: ascertain whether you suffer strong carnal impulses (pricking stings) and whether you possess the gift of continency; these facts determine whether marriage is advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continency as criterion for marrying
rubrics_metrics.description: If in this carnal strife and debate of yours have you obtained from God the gift and special grace of continency? ... My counsel to you in that case, my friend, is that you marry; for you should rather choose to marry once than to burn still in fires of concupiscence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee advises that one without the ability to remain continent should marry to avoid ongoing sexual torment. The recommendation is pragmatic: marry if you cannot restrain your passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a wife for piety and virtuous upbringing, not merely rank or wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: You shall never be a cuckold ... if you make choice of one of a commendable extraction, descended of honest parents, and instructed in all piety and virtue--such a one as hath not at any time haunted or frequented the company or conversation of those that are of corrupt and depraved manners, one loving and fearing God...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee's spouse-selection rule emphasizes lineage of virtue, piety, avoidance of corrupt company, and religious devotion over material wealth or noble birth. The ideal wife is described at length; her fear of God and conscience will restrain adultery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Husband must lead by virtuous example
rubrics_metrics.description: Your behaviour is to be such, that you are to go before her in a good example, by entertaining her unfeignedly with a conjugal amity, by continually approving yourself in all your words and actions a faithful and discreet husband; and by living ... devoutly, virtuously, and chastely ... as you would have her ... deport and demean herself towards you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure fidelity and moral household order, the husband should exemplify the virtues he expects: public and private piety, constancy, and visible good conduct. The mirror/metaphor of sun and moon is used: the wife reflects the husband's virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer to divine providence as a canonical exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When I tell you,--'If it please God,'--do I to you any wrong therein? ... Is it not expedient that what we propose unto ourselves be still referred to what shall be disposed of by the sacred will of God?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee frames pronouncements with the canonical reservation 'if it please God', recommending that major undertakings be humbly referred to divine will; this is presented as both reverent and prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wine (in excess) to abate lust
rubrics_metrics.description: First, By the means of wine. ... when I say ... wine abateth lust, my meaning is, wine immoderately taken; for by intemperancy ... there is brought upon the body ... a chillness in the blood, a slackening in the sinews ... all which are great lets and impediments to the act of generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rondibilis (physician) notes that excessive drinking produces physical debility and reduced sexual potency, thereby diminishing sexual desire and capability; moderate drinking has opposite (arousing) effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of certain drugs, herbs, and substances to dampen libido
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, The fervency of lust is abated by certain drugs, plants, herbs, and roots ... which make the taker cold, maleficiated, unfit for, and unable to perform the act of generation ... such as water-lily, agnus castus, willow-twigs, hemp-stalks, honeysuckle, chaste tree, mandrake, bennet, ... the skin of a hippopotam, and many other such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medicalized prescription: certain ingestible substances (listed) are said to 'benumb, mortify, and beclumpse' the seminal fluids or obstruct their passage; conversely other ingredients heat and stimulate. Effects depend on dose and individual constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent labour and continual toiling as a cure for lust
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, The ardour of lechery is very much subdued and mated by frequent labour and continual toiling. For by painful exercises and laborious working so great a dissolution is brought upon the whole body ... that nature ... more heedfully regardeth ... preservation ... than the propagating of the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical exertion dissipates the bodily resources and nervous/sexual energy that feed lust; being constantly busy or physically taxed reduces sexual appetite. The text contrasts industriousness with idleness, which breeds luxury and lechery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eager study and intellectual occupation blunt sexual impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourthly, The tickling pricks of incontinency are blunted by an eager study; for from thence proceedeth an incredible resolution of the spirits, that oftentimes there do not remain so many behind as may suffice to push ... the generative resudation ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained intellectual absorption redirects vital spirits and attention toward mental faculties, leaving insufficient animal spirits for sexual excitement; philosophers and Muses are portrayed as perpetually chaste because of their studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent repetition of the sexual act reduces ardour
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifthly, By the too frequent reiteration of the act of venery. ... Father Scyllino ... calleth by the name of maceration and taming of the flesh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated sexual activity can exhaust or 'macerate' the flesh so that desire diminishes; this is offered as a practical (though blunt) method to tame carnal appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid idleness; idleness predisposes to adultery
rubrics_metrics.description: On the other part, in opposition and repugnancy hereto, the philosophers say that idleness is the mother of luxury. ... When it was asked Ovid, Why Aegisthus became an adulterer? he made no other answer but this, Because he was idle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral prescription is social and behavioral: keep occupied (work, study, religion) because idleness fosters lewdness and makes one vulnerable to adulterous conduct. This supports the labour and study remedies already given.
